title: Al-Buruj: the constellations
hookLine: the people of the ditch who were burned for their faith (85:4–8)
last: AT-TARIQ — EVERY SOUL HAS A GUARDIAN.

lines: BURUJ — THE TOWERS OF THE SKY.
cards: Dubai's skyline has a needle in the middle of it: the Burj Khalifa. Burj means tower.
In the plural, buruj, it's the name of the surah before At-Tariq, and there it means the great towers of the night sky: the constellations, the mansions of the stars. The surah opens looking up.
But it quickly looks down, into a trench in the ground, at a scene that is hard to hear: people burned for what they believed, while others sat and watched.

teach.h: THE SKY, THE DAY, THE WITNESS.
teach.b: Surah eighty-five swears by the sky with its constellations, by the promised Day, and by the witness and what is witnessed.

teach.h: AL-UKHDUD — THE PEOPLE OF THE DITCH.
teach.b: Then verse four: destroyed were the people of the ditch, al-ukhdud, the fire full of fuel, as they sat around it, witnessing what they were doing to the believers.
Verse eight gives the only charge against the victims: they had nothing against them except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised. The Qur'an doesn't name who they were.
The commentators offer two main accounts.

teach.h: THE BOY AND THE KING, OR NAJRAN.
teach.b: One is a long hadith in Muslim's collection about a boy, a king and a monk: the boy's faith spreads to a whole town, and the king has trenches dug and fires lit for anyone who won't turn back.

The other, told by Ibn Ishaq and the commentators, connects it to Najran, in southern Arabia, where a king named Dhu Nuwas is reported to have killed the Christians of the town who would not give up their faith.

In that reading, the believers the Qur'an honors here were Christians. Either way, the surah doesn't glorify the fire, or ask anyone to seek it. It condemns the people who lit it, and it sees the ones who stood firm.
Verse ten leaves a door open: those who persecuted believers, and then did not repent, face the punishment. And then did not repent.
Even there, the way back isn't shut. People of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief, and still are. The surah keeps them in view.

how: Muslims remember the people of the ditch as believers who held firm under persecution; the hadith of the boy and the king is a well-known story told to children and in sermons about steadfastness.

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: the constellations, towers of the sky
the ditch, the trench of fire

s: the Qur'an names the people of the ditch
it doesn't. commentators offer the boy and the king (Muslim) or the Christians of Najran.
in one reading, the believers burned were Christians of Najran
Ibn Ishaq and some commentators connect the story to Dhu Nuwas and the Christians of Najran.
the surah leaves no way back for the persecutors
verse ten says: and then did not repent. the door is still named.

games.q: the believers in the ditch were accused of something. what does verse eight say it was?
o: only that they believed in God
games.why: nothing except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised (85:8). faith was the only charge.

practice: Hold in mind people who are suffering for their beliefs right now, somewhere in the world; no names needed, just a family, a place of worship, a person in a cell. Hold them steadily, the way the surah does, without looking away.
If you pray, you can ask for them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Buruj. The constellations, the towers of the sky, and the name of Surah eighty-five, which remembers the people of the ditch. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the ditch or trench, from kh-d-d, a furrow cut in the ground (Qur'an 85:4).

carryVoice: Your line: faith under fire. Their only charge was that they believed. Day two hundred four.
